title: Pre-Qualification vs Pre-Approval: Choosing a Mortgage Lender
description: Pre-qualification vs pre-approval explained, plus how to compare Loan Estimates from several lenders and what to ask when choosing a mortgage lender.
body:
Before you tour homes in Williamson County or anywhere else in Middle Tennessee, it helps to talk with a lender. The terms get mixed up, though, and the choice of lender affects what you pay. This post covers the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval, how to compare lenders, and where an agent's referral fits in.

## Pre-qualification vs pre-approval

{{img:0}}

These two steps sound alike, but they are not the same thing.

A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow. It is based on information you tell a lender, such as income, debts and savings. It is a useful starting point for setting a rough budget.

A pre-approval goes further. The lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter. That is the key difference: in a pre-approval, someone has actually looked at your paperwork.

A pre-approval letter is still not a final loan commitment. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting, and your finances staying the same until closing. So the letter is a step in the process, not the finish line.

## Why get Loan Estimates from more than one lender

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) encourages borrowers to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender and compare them, because interest rates and fees can differ from lender to lender. Their [Owning a Home guides](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) walk through the process in plain language.

After you apply, a lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days. It is a standard three-page form, so estimates from different lenders can be compared side by side. You are looking at the same layout each time, which makes differences easier to spot.

For a sense of the backdrop, Freddie Mac reported an average 30-year fixed mortgage rate of 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01 (via FRED). That is a national average. The rate you are quoted depends on your own situation and the lender, which is exactly why comparing matters.

### Will shopping around hurt your credit?

Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Comparing lenders close together is usually less harmful to your credit than spreading the applications out over months. Ask each lender how this works for your situation, since I can't tell you how it will affect your own score.

## What to compare on each Loan Estimate

{{img:1}}

Don't stop at the interest rate. Put the estimates next to each other and look at:

- The interest rate and the loan type being quoted
- Lender fees and other closing costs
- Whether mortgage insurance is included
- The estimated monthly payment
- The cash you would need to bring to closing

Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. Private mortgage insurance is typically required on conventional loans when the down payment is under 20 percent, so check how it shows up in each quote.

If you want to see how a rate changes a payment, try the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator) with a few different numbers.

### Loan programs worth asking about

Different loan types come with different rules. FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent. VA loans typically require no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee may apply. You can read the basics on the [VA home loans](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/) page.

The [Tennessee Housing Development Agency](https://www.thda.org) (THDA) offers home loan programs through participating lenders. Ask any lender you are considering whether they take part. Not every lender does.

I can explain how these programs work in general, but whether one fits your finances is a question for a lender.

## Types of lenders

Mortgage lenders include banks, credit unions, mortgage brokers and online lenders. A mortgage broker compares offers from several lenders on your behalf. Each type works a little differently, so it is fair to ask any of them how they are paid, how fast they close, and who you will talk to when you have a question.

## Asking your agent for lender names

Your real estate agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work. That can save you some searching, and it is reasonable to ask.

Here is the part that matters: you choose your own lender. You are free to use any lender you like, and no one should pressure you toward a particular one. Treat a referral as one input, not the answer. Get a Loan Estimate from the lender your agent mentions and from at least one or two others, then compare them yourself.

I can't recommend or endorse any single lender in a blog post, and I wouldn't want you to take a name on faith anyway. Do your own homework and make your own call.

## Keep your finances steady after you apply

Once you apply, a few habits help keep your file clean through closing. Avoid opening new credit, financing furniture, or changing jobs from the time you apply for a loan through closing. If something has to change, tell your lender first.

Also, a lender must send the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before closing. Compare it with your Loan Estimate and ask questions about anything that looks different. When it is time to send funds, wire fraud is real. Verify wire instructions by phone using a number you already trust, and never rely on emailed wire instructions.

## How the market fits in

Your budget and your lender are only part of the picture. For the Nashville metro, Redfin reported a median sale price of $461,491 for the 4 weeks ending 2026-09-27, with 5.6 months of supply. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers. Numbers vary by town, so I keep local figures on the [market data page](/market-data).

## Next steps

A simple order of operations: get pre-qualified for a rough budget, then get pre-approved with documents, and request Loan Estimates from more than one lender so you can compare them. If you want to talk through the process or start looking at homes, fill out the [Get Matched form](/buy#form) and I will schedule a call within the next 48 hours. You can also reach me through the [contact page](/contact).

faq.q: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?
faq.a: A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow, based on information you tell a lender. A pre-approval goes further: the lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter.

faq.q: Is a pre-approval letter a guarantee of a loan?
faq.a: No. A pre-approval letter is not a final loan commitment. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting and your finances staying the same until closing.

faq.q: Should I get Loan Estimates from more than one lender?
faq.a: The CFPB encourages borrowers to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender and compare them, because interest rates and fees can differ. The Loan Estimate is a standard three-page form, so you can compare them side by side.

faq.q: Does comparing mortgage lenders hurt my credit?
faq.a: Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Ask each lender how this works for your situation.

faq.q: Do I have to use the lender my agent suggests?
faq.a: No. Your agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work, but you choose your own lender and are free to use any lender you like.
